composition: Duplex lightweight steel of nominal composition Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.8C (all in wt.%), i.e. a Fe-based matrix alloyed with 15 wt.% Mn, 10 wt.% Al and 0.8 wt.% C and containing no Ni. This grade was selected specifically as the Ni-free counterpart of Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.8C-5Ni so that the properties of FeAl-type B2 (Ni-free) could be compared with NiAl-type B2, and to isolate the intrinsic contribution of the κ-carbide (L1′2) formed in both grades. Mn and Al provide the density reduction and drive the formation of the ordered precipitates (κ-carbide and B2), while C stabilizes the perovskite-type κ-carbide. Note: in Table 1 and Table 2 this Ni-free alloy is printed as Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.5C, whereas the text states 0.8 wt.% C.
conclusions: For the Ni-free Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.8C alloy annealed at 500 °C, the precipitate-bearing structures measured by nano-indentation are γ + κ = 6.8 GPa and α + κ = 5.3 GPa, both well above the ≈4 GPa (γ) and ≈3 GPa (α) of the solution-treated parent phases and below the B2-bearing structures of the Ni-containing grade. The 500 °C treatment is the low-temperature extreme of the study, at which the Ni-free α phase holds micrometer-sized needle-like κ-carbides instead of the B2 stringer bands found in the 5 wt.% Ni grade (10.1 GPa at 500 °C); this replacement of nano-sized B2 discs by micrometre-sized κ needles in the Ni-free alloy lowers the hardness relative to the Ni-containing alloy, which the authors explain by the weaker Fe–Al bonding of FeAl-type B2 and by the Mn dependence of κ hardness. The results show that the room-temperature mechanical response of these lightweight steels is governed by the type, composition and size of the ordered precipitates, making the nanomechanical characterization of individual phases (nano-indentation plus DFT) a useful basis for alloy and processing design. Practical significance: this Ni-free chemistry achieves the desired precipitate-hardened structure with a minimum amount of Ni, which is attractive from an economic perspective for light-weighting transport structures; the study also notes that the earlier observation of low ductility (elongation ≈10%) at low annealing temperature points to a strength–ductility trade-off that improves at higher annealing temperatures.
mechanisms: Solution treatment at 1250 °C for 35 min followed by water quenching produces a supersaturated duplex γ + α matrix; the subsequent 500 °C isothermal anneal then precipitates the ordered phases (cuboid and needle-like κ-carbide, and coarse B2) that harden the matrix.

Because the alloy contains no Ni, at low annealing temperatures (500–700 °C) the α (ferrite) phase cannot transform into Ni-Al-type B2 stringer bands; instead it retains the α matrix with needle-like κ-carbides, which is why this 500 °C Ni-free sample differs microstructurally from the 5 wt.% Ni grade annealed at the same temperature.

The hardness of the needle-like κ-carbides formed in the α phase is controlled by their Mn content: κ particles precipitated at 700 °C contain more Mn (≈24.8 wt.%) than those formed at 500 °C (≈18.4 wt.%), and the higher Mn content raises the formation energy, lattice parameter and magnetic response of the κ-phase, producing harder κ particles — this explains the experimentally measured increase of α + κ hardness from 5.3 GPa (500 °C) to 6.7 GPa (700 °C).

First-principles (DFT) calculations show that placing the C atom in the octahedral interstitial site of the L1′2 structure rigidifies Fe3AlC relative to Fe3Al, a direct manifestation of strong Fe–C bonds along the <100> directions; the C insertion also increases the elastic constants while it has a lesser effect on the Fe3Al-L12 phase.

Substituting Fe by Mn in the κ-carbide increases the lattice parameter (3.78 Å for Fe2MnAlC up to 3.84 Å for Mn3AlC, the larger Mn atomic radius rMn = 1.61 Å versus rFe = 1.56 Å) and raises the bulk modulus, shear modulus and Young's modulus, because Mn–C bonds are stronger than Fe–C bonds; this supports the experimentally observed hardening of κ with increasing Mn content and explains why Fe3AlC behaves as an un-shearable precipitate.

Orowan strengthening: the increase in shear stress is inversely proportional to the precipitate diameter (Δτ ∝ R^−1.25), so finer precipitates offer greater resistance to shear; this rationalizes why the nano-sized precipitates observed at higher annealing temperatures give higher hardness values in these low-density steels.

For a given matrix, any structure containing ordered precipitates is substantially harder than the parent γ or α phase, because the ordered κ-carbide and B2 particles (and their interfaces with the matrix) resist shear more strongly than the disordered solid solution; consequently γ + κ (6.8 GPa) and α + κ (5.3 GPa) at 500 °C are far harder than the solution-treated γ (≈4 GPa) and α (≈3 GPa).

In the Ni-free alloy the low-Al FeAl-type B2 particles formed in γ and the nano-sized B2 formed in α do not differ much in hardness (9.2 vs 8.9 GPa at 900 °C; 9.0 vs 8.3 GPa at 1050 °C), which the authors relate to Al partitioning — Al is an α stabiliser, so B2 in γ is Al-poorer and was anticipated to be harder — a compositional effect that also controls the temperature dependence of B2 hardness in this grade.

The Al-rich FeAl-type B2 of the Ni-free grade forms weaker/less exothermic bonds than the NiAl-type B2 of the Ni-containing grade (lower elastic constants and lower magnitude enthalpy of formation for Fe-Al than for (Fe,Ni)-Al), which is why adding Ni raises the peak hardness of the B2-bearing structures from 7.2 GPa to 9 GPa in both austenite and ferrite; this bonding argument is the basis for the lower hardness of the Ni-free 500 °C structure relative to its Ni-containing counterpart.
microstructure: After annealing at 500 °C the Ni-free alloy has a duplex γ + α (austenite fcc + ferrite bcc) matrix containing four phases in total (γ, α, κ-carbide, B2). The γ (austenite) grains contain nano-sized cuboid κ-carbide blocks (< 100 nm), identified as L1′2/Fe3AlC-type ordered fcc, together with coarse FeAl-type B2 intermetallic particles 2–4 μm in size distributed in the matrix and at grain boundaries; coarse B2 particles (2–4 μm) are present at all four annealing temperatures in this grade. The α (ferrite) regions contain micron-sized needle-like κ-carbide particles of width 200 ± 33 nm and average size ≈ 1.5 μm. Crucially, at 500 °C (and 700 °C) the Ni-free sample displays α + needle-like κ-carbides instead of the B2 stringer bands that form in the Ni-containing counterpart at the same temperatures; this morphology change is the key microstructural difference between the two grades at low annealing temperature.
processing: Processing lineage: (1) the experimental alloys were melted in an induction furnace; (2) solution heat treatment for 35 min at 1250 °C in a protective argon atmosphere, then water quenched; (3) the material was cut into specimens 3 mm (length) × 3 mm (width) × 1 mm (thickness) for nano-indentation; (4) isothermal annealing at 500 °C — the lowest of the four annealing temperatures studied (500, 700, 900 and 1050 °C). The holding time of the annealing treatment is not explicitly reported in the text, and no cooling medium is specified for it. The 500 °C condition is thus the low-temperature end of the annealing series, below the temperature range (≥900 °C) at which nano-sized B2 discs replace the low-temperature κ-carbides.
properties: Nano-indentation (constant loading/unloading rate 500 μN s⁻¹, maximum load 10000 μN, hold time 20 s, each phase measured at least 25 times, arrays of 50–70 indentations; specimen 3 mm × 3 mm × 1 mm) gave composite hardness values for the precipitate-bearing structures of this 500 °C Ni-free sample: γ + κ (austenite with nano cuboid κ-carbide) = 6.8 GPa and α + κ (ferrite with needle-like κ-carbide) = 5.3 GPa. For reference, the parent phases of the solution-treated Ni-free alloy measure γ ≈ 4 GPa and α ≈ 3 GPa, so the precipitate-bearing composites are markedly harder than the parent matrix. The paper stresses that nano-indentation cannot resolve isolated nano-sized precipitates and therefore yields compound matrix + particle hardness values. Characterization techniques applied to the materials include TEM (JEOL 2000FX, bright-field imaging and selected-area diffraction patterns; thin foils twin-jet electro-polished in 10% perchloric acid + 90% ethanol at 25 V), FE-SEM (Carl Zeiss Sigma, 20 kV) with X-ray EDS on 5% nital-etched specimens, nano-indentation, and DFT/ab-initio calculations (Quantum-ESPRESSO) for the κ-carbide.
summary: Ni-free duplex low-density steel Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.8C (wt.%) in the condition obtained by solution treatment at 1250 °C followed by isothermal annealing at 500 °C. The sample is one of the two grades (Ni-free and 5 wt.% Ni) used in the paper to compare the nano-mechanical properties of the ordered FeAl-type B2 intermetallic and the κ-carbide (L1′2) as a function of annealing temperature; because the nano-sized cuboid κ particles in austenite are too small to indent individually, its κ-phase properties were assessed by DFT and by composite nano-indentation of the surrounding matrix.
unmapped: The paper registers a composition inconsistency for this grade: the text and abstract give Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.8C (wt.%), while Tables 1 and 2 label the Ni-free alloy Fe-15Mn-10Al-0.5C; the provided aliases retain both forms.
The annealing holding time at 500 °C is not explicitly reported in the text, and no cooling medium is given for the annealing step.

The γ-phase nano-sized cuboid κ-carbide of this sample could not be measured by nano-indentation because of its nano-size (equivalent result exists for the Ni-containing sample), which is the stated reason the authors resorted to first-principles calculations of the elastic constants of κ-carbide as a function of Mn content.

The nano-indentation measurement volume (indent size/shape-dependent plastic zone) introduces an indentation size effect that may obscure the real influence of individual precipitate sizes on the composite hardness; the authors state that different indentors or loads would be required to isolate the size effect.

DFT-derived elastic parameters for the κ-carbide and related compounds of relevance to the Ni-free alloy include B0, shear modulus G, Young's moduli E100/E111 and a factor of anisotropy Cα > 1 (e.g. Fe3AlC(sp): B0 = 216/−206 GPa, G = 175/−168.5 GPa, E100 = 477/−397 GPa, E111 = 217/−227 GPa, Cα = 2.39/−2.47; Mn3AlC higher still), showing that the C-containing κ-phase is strongly anisotropic whereas FeAl-B2 is nearly isotropic (Cα ≈ 0.54).
